title: OA 1 — Market Data and ML Foundations
description: Mock data-science internship assessment: ML foundations, probability and inference, AI search, market-data SQL (Securities / MarketQuotes / Trades), tick cleaning in pandas, and array/two-pointer and sliding-window DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate's browser; reveal solutions only after the whole attempt has been submitted or timed out.

questions.statement: A depth-unrestricted decision tree predicting next-day volume has a training RMSE of 0.4 and a validation RMSE of 3.9. Which action is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Report the training RMSE because it is the lower and therefore better estimate
Remove the validation set so the model can use more data for training
Constrain the model (e.g., limit tree depth or require a minimum leaf size) and re-check validation error
Add more tree depth so training error becomes exactly zero

solution.explanation: A large train/validation gap signals high variance (overfitting). Restricting model capacity or adding regularization usually narrows the gap. Making the tree deeper would worsen it; training error is an optimistic estimate and must not be reported as performance.

questions.statement: A fraud classifier scored 1,000 transactions and produced: TP = 30, FP = 20, FN = 10, TN = 940. What is its F1 score (to three decimals)?

solution.explanation: Precision = 30/(30+20) = 0.60 and recall = 30/(30+10) = 0.75, so F1 = 2·0.6·0.75/(0.6+0.75) = 0.667. 0.97 is accuracy ((30+940)/1000), which is dominated by the many true negatives; 0.60 and 0.75 are only the components.

questions.statement: For a k-nearest-neighbours classifier the team recorded: k=1 → train error 0%, 5-fold CV error 22%; k=15 → train 12%, CV 14%; k=200 → train 25%, CV 26%. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: k=1 is best because its training error is lowest
k=1 overfits (high variance); k=200 underfits (high bias); k=15 gives the best bias-variance trade-off of the three
k=200 is best because its training and CV errors are nearly equal
All three are equivalent because CV error is always higher than training error

solution.explanation: Choose by validation/CV error, not training error. k=1 memorises noise (0% train, 22% CV). k=200 is too smooth so even training error is high (high bias). Similar train and CV error alone does not mean the model is good if both are high.

questions.statement: You are building a model at market close to predict whether tomorrow's closing price will be higher than today's. One candidate feature is 'tomorrow's total traded volume'. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Include it: more predictive features always improve the model
Include it only in the training set and leave it out of the test set
Include it but standardise it so the leakage has less effect
Exclude it: it is not available at prediction time, so it leaks future information and will inflate offline metrics

solution.explanation: A feature must be computable at the moment of prediction. Tomorrow's volume is only known after the target period, so offline scores would be unrealistically good and the model would fail in production. Scaling or train-only inclusion does not fix leakage.

questions.statement: A linear regression has 200 correlated input features and the analyst wants an automatic feature subset where many coefficients are exactly zero. Which method is best suited?

options.text: Increasing the learning rate of the optimiser
L1-regularised regression (Lasso)
L2-regularised regression (Ridge), which sets many coefficients exactly to zero
Ordinary least squares with no penalty

solution.explanation: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero and tends to drive some coefficients exactly to zero, giving sparsity. Ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero. OLS has no shrinkage; the learning rate affects optimisation, not the penalty.

questions.statement: Which model's predictions are least affected if every numeric feature is multiplied by a different positive constant (feature rescaling)?

options.text: k-nearest neighbours, because distances are scale invariant
Ridge regression, because the penalty is applied per example
A decision tree, because splits depend only on the ordering of feature values
A support vector machine with an RBF kernel

solution.explanation: Trees choose thresholds on single features, so positive rescaling only moves the thresholds. Distance-based models (kNN, RBF-SVM) change which points are near; penalised linear models change how much each coefficient is penalised.

questions.statement: 2% of trades are fraudulent. A detector flags 90% of fraudulent trades and also flags 5% of legitimate trades. A randomly chosen trade is flagged. What is the probability that it is fraudulent?

options.text: About 47%
About 26.9%
About 2%
About 90%

solution.explanation: P(F|flag) = 0.02·0.90 / (0.02·0.90 + 0.98·0.05) = 0.018/0.067 ≈ 0.269. The base rate is low, so most flags are false alarms even with a good detector; 90% is the recall P(flag|F), not the posterior.

questions.statement: Daily returns of a stock are modelled as Normal with mean 0.10% and standard deviation 1.50%. Approximately what is the probability that tomorrow's return is below −1.90%?

options.text: About 18.2%
About 9.1%
About 0.9%
About 4.8%

solution.explanation: z = (−1.90 − 0.10)/1.50 = −1.333, and Φ(−1.333) ≈ 0.091. Forgetting to subtract the mean (z = −1.27) or using the wrong tail gives other options; 18.2% would be a two-sided probability.

questions.statement: A random sample of n = 64 order latencies has mean 12.0 ms and sample standard deviation 8.0 ms. Using the normal approximation, what is an approximate 95% confidence interval for the true mean latency?

solution.explanation: SE = 8/√64 = 1, so the interval is 12 ± 1.96·1 = (10.04, 13.96). (4.16, 19.84) wrongly uses the standard deviation instead of the standard error; (8.08, 15.92) uses SE = 2 (n=16).

questions.statement: A random variable X (daily P&L in thousands) has E[X] = 4 and Var(X) = 9. What are the mean and variance of Y = 2X + 3?

options.text: E[Y] = 11 and Var(Y) = 39
E[Y] = 11 and Var(Y) = 36
E[Y] = 11 and Var(Y) = 18
E[Y] = 8 and Var(Y) = 36

solution.explanation: E[2X+3] = 2·4 + 3 = 11. Adding a constant does not change variance and scaling by 2 multiplies variance by 2² = 4, so Var(Y) = 4·9 = 36.

questions.statement: Trade sizes are right-skewed with standard deviation 30 shares. The standard error of the sample mean is computed from samples of n = 100. If the desk instead samples n = 400 independent trades, what happens to the standard error?

options.text: It falls from 3 to 1.5, i.e., it is halved
It stays at 3 because the population is skewed
It falls from 30 to 7.5
It falls from 3 to 0.75, i.e., it is quartered

solution.explanation: SE = σ/√n: 30/10 = 3 for n = 100 and 30/20 = 1.5 for n = 400. Quadrupling n only halves SE. Skewness affects how fast the sampling distribution becomes normal, not the SE formula.

questions.statement: Which statement about A* search is correct?

options.text: A* ignores the cost already paid and ranks nodes only by the heuristic
With an admissible heuristic (one that never overestimates the true remaining cost) A* returns a lowest-cost path
A* always expands fewer nodes than breadth-first search regardless of the heuristic
A* is optimal for any heuristic as long as it is non-negative

solution.explanation: A* orders nodes by f = g + h. If h is admissible (and the graph search is handled consistently), the first goal popped is optimal. A non-negative but overestimating heuristic can mislead the search; ranking only by h is greedy best-first search, which is not optimal.

questions.statement: A team has two years of unlabelled order-flow records and wants to discover groups of traders with similar behaviour. Which approach fits?

options.text: Reinforcement learning, since there is a reward in every trade
Unsupervised learning, e.g., k-means or hierarchical clustering on behavioural features
Supervised classification with logistic regression, since logistic regression works on any dataset
Supervised regression to predict trader IDs

solution.explanation: With no labels and an exploratory goal of finding structure, clustering is the natural tool. Logistic regression needs labelled targets; there is no sequential decision problem or reward signal specified for reinforcement learning.

questions.statement: A feed-forward network has three dense layers but every layer uses the identity (linear) activation. What is the effect on the function the network can represent?

options.text: It becomes equivalent to a decision tree of depth three
It can approximate any continuous function because it has three layers
It is equivalent to a single linear transformation, so depth adds no representational power
It can represent XOR because depth increases capacity

solution.explanation: Composition of linear maps is linear: W3(W2(W1x)) = (W3W2W1)x. Non-linear activations (ReLU, tanh, ...) are what let depth model non-linear patterns like XOR.

questions.statement: In a two-player game search, alpha-beta pruning is applied to minimax. Which statement is true?

options.text: It increases the number of nodes explored but makes each cheaper
It only works if every node has exactly two children
It returns the same root value as plain minimax while potentially exploring fewer nodes
It returns an approximate value that can differ from minimax, trading accuracy for speed

solution.explanation: Alpha-beta only prunes branches that cannot influence the final decision, so the minimax value is unchanged; the savings depend on move ordering. It works for any branching factor.

questions.statement: Table P(price) contains the values 10, NULL, 20, NULL, 30. What does SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(price), AVG(price) FROM P return?

solution.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (5); COUNT(price) ignores NULLs (3); AVG ignores NULLs, so (10+20+30)/3 = 20, not 60/5 = 12.

questions.statement: A query lists every security with its filled trades: SELECT s.ticker, t.trade_id FROM Securities s LEFT JOIN Trades t ON t.security_id = s.security_id WHERE t.status = 'FILLED'. Securities that have no trades at all are missing from the output. Why?

options.text: Securities without trades violate a foreign-key constraint
The WHERE condition on the right-hand table is false (NULL) for the null-extended rows, so they are filtered out; the status test belongs in the ON clause
SQL removes NULL rows automatically after any join
LEFT JOIN only returns rows that have a match in both tables

solution.explanation: The WHERE clause is evaluated after the join; for unmatched securities t.status is NULL, and NULL = 'FILLED' is not true, so those rows disappear and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN. Moving the predicate into ON preserves them.

options.text: false false
true false
false true
true true

solution.explanation: `new String(...)` creates two distinct objects, so `==` (reference comparison) is false, while `equals` compares character content and is true.

options.text: It does not compile because label() is not overridden
[ORDER]
LIMIT
[LIMIT]

solution.explanation: `label()` is inherited, but the call `tag()` inside it is dispatched at run time on the actual object (a LimitOrder), so the overridden version runs. This is run-time polymorphism.

questions.statement: An order-entry rule accepts quantities from 1 to 1,000 inclusive. Which set of test inputs best applies boundary value analysis?

solution.explanation: Defects cluster at the edges, so test just outside and exactly on each boundary: 0 and 1 for the lower edge, 1000 and 1001 for the upper edge. Mid-range values add little boundary coverage.

questions.statement: Rows 2–6 of a sheet hold Ticker (col A), Side (col B), Qty (col C): AAPL/BUY/100, AAPL/SELL/40, MSFT/BUY/70, AAPL/BUY/25, MSFT/SELL/10. What does =SUMIFS(C2:C6, A2:A6, "AAPL", B2:B6, "BUY") return?

solution.explanation: SUMIFS adds Qty only where all criteria hold: AAPL and BUY → rows 2 and 5, 100 + 25 = 125. 165 would include the AAPL SELL row; 195 also adds the MSFT BUY row (100+70+25).

questions.statement: A minute-by-minute price feed for a stock reads 100.2, 100.3, 1003.1, 100.4, 100.5. What is the best first action?

options.text: Replace every value in the series with the series mean
Treat 1003.1 as a probable decimal-shift error: flag it, compare with bid/ask or another source, and correct or exclude it with a documented rule
Delete the whole day's data without investigation
Keep it, because extreme values are always real market information

solution.explanation: A tenfold jump that reverts immediately is a classic bad-tick pattern. Flag and validate against independent data, then apply a documented fix. Blindly keeping, mean-imputing everything, or deleting the whole day are all unjustified.

questions.title: Average Mid-Price per NASDAQ Security
questions.statement:
A data engineer needs a quality-checked summary of end-of-day quotes for NASDAQ-listed securities.

Write one `SELECT` that joins `Securities` and `MarketQuotes` and returns, for each security with `exchange = 'NASDAQ'`:

* `ticker`
* `valid_quotes` – number of quotes in which **both** `bid` and `ask` are non-NULL
* `avg_mid` – the average of the mid-price `(bid + ask) / 2` over those valid quotes, rounded to 2 decimals
* `max_volume` – the largest `volume` among those valid quotes

Rules: ignore quotes with a missing bid or ask entirely (they must not count towards any column); return only securities with **at least 2** valid quotes. Sort by `avg_mid` descending, then `ticker` ascending.

tables.name: MarketQuotes
tables.description: At most one end-of-day quote per security per date.

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Securities (
  security_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  ticker      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  sector      TEXT NOT NULL,
  exchange    TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE MarketQuotes (
  quote_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  quote_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  bid         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  ask         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  volume      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (security_id, quote_date)
);
CREATE TABLE Trades (
  trade_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  trader_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  trade_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  side        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (side IN ('BUY','SELL')),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  price       REAL NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('FILLED','PENDING','REJECTED','CANCELLED'))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT s.ticker, COUNT(*) AS valid_quotes, 0.0 AS avg_mid, 0 AS max_volume
FROM Securities s
JOIN MarketQuotes q ON q.security_id = s.security_id
-- TODO: filters, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: ticker, valid_quotes, avg_mid, max_volume. Ordered by avg_mid DESC, ticker ASC.

publicTests.description: Second sample with a single-quote security and a spread-heavy day

hiddenTests.description: No valid quotes for NASDAQ securities (empty result expected)
Ties in avg_mid between two securities (tie-break on ticker)
Randomised 8 securities, many NULL bid/ask values

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT s.ticker,
       COUNT(*)                          AS valid_quotes,
       ROUND(AVG((q.bid + q.ask) / 2.0), 2) AS avg_mid,
       MAX(q.volume)                     AS max_volume
FROM Securities s
JOIN MarketQuotes q ON q.security_id = s.security_id
WHERE s.exchange = 'NASDAQ'
  AND q.bid IS NOT NULL AND q.ask IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY s.security_id, s.ticker
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_mid DESC, s.ticker ASC;
solution.explanation: Join the tables, drop quotes with a NULL bid or ask in WHERE (so they affect no aggregate), group by security, keep groups with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2, and order by the rounded average then ticker. Using COUNT(q.quote_id) without the NULL filter over-counts; filtering with HAVING instead of WHERE would leave NULL quotes inside the aggregates.

questions.title: Execution Slippage versus Same-Day Mid
questions.statement:
The best-execution team compares each **filled** trade with the mid-price quoted for the same security on the same date.

For a trade matched to a quote with non-NULL `bid` and `ask`, define `mid = (bid + ask) / 2` and the **slippage** (positive = worse for the trader):

* `BUY`: `price - mid`
* `SELL`: `mid - price`

Using `Trades`, `Securities` and `MarketQuotes` (match quotes on `security_id` and `quote_date = trade_date`), return one row per security that has at least one matched filled trade:

`sector, ticker, matched_trades, avg_slippage, sector_rank`

* `matched_trades` – count of matched filled trades
* `avg_slippage` – average slippage rounded to 4 decimals
* `sector_rank` – `RANK()` of the security **within its sector**, ordered by the reported `avg_slippage` **ascending** (lowest slippage = rank 1; ties share a rank)

Only trades with `status = 'FILLED'` count. Sort by `sector`, `sector_rank`, `ticker`.

tables.description: At most one end-of-day quote per security per date.

CREATE TABLE Securities (

  ticker      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,

  exchange    TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE MarketQuotes (
  quote_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  quote_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  bid         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  ask         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  volume      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (security_id, quote_date)
);
CREATE TABLE Trades (
  trade_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  trader_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  trade_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  side        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (side IN ('BUY','SELL')),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  price       REAL NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('FILLED','PENDING','REJECTED','CANCELLED'))
);
questions.starterQuery:
WITH matched AS (
  SELECT s.sector, s.ticker, 0.0 AS slip
  FROM Trades t
  JOIN Securities s ON s.security_id = t.security_id
  -- TODO: join MarketQuotes, compute slippage per side
)
SELECT sector, ticker, COUNT(*) AS matched_trades, 0.0 AS avg_slippage, 1 AS sector_rank
FROM matched
GROUP BY sector, ticker;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: sector, ticker, matched_trades, avg_slippage, sector_rank. Order: sector, sector_rank, ticker.

hiddenTests.description: Trades without same-day quote or with NULL bid/ask are excluded
Two securities in one sector with equal slippage (RANK ties) plus a single-security sector

solution.referenceSolution:
WITH matched AS (
  SELECT s.sector, s.ticker,
         CASE t.side WHEN 'BUY'  THEN t.price - (q.bid + q.ask) / 2.0
                     ELSE (q.bid + q.ask) / 2.0 - t.price END AS slip
  FROM Trades t
  JOIN Securities   s ON s.security_id = t.security_id
  JOIN MarketQuotes q ON q.security_id = t.security_id AND q.quote_date = t.trade_date
  WHERE t.status = 'FILLED' AND q.bid IS NOT NULL AND q.ask IS NOT NULL
),
agg AS (
  SELECT sector, ticker, COUNT(*) AS matched_trades, ROUND(AVG(slip), 4) AS avg_slippage
  FROM matched GROUP BY sector, ticker
)
SELECT sector, ticker, matched_trades, avg_slippage,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY sector ORDER BY avg_slippage ASC) AS sector_rank
FROM agg
ORDER BY sector, sector_rank, ticker;
solution.explanation: Three-way join on security and date; CASE flips the sign for SELL. Aggregate per security first (CTE), then apply RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY sector ORDER BY avg_slippage). Ranking after rounding means equal reported slippages share a rank.

questions.starterQuery:
UPDATE Trades
SET status = 'REJECTED'
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  -- TODO: only when no supporting quote exists
  AND 1 = 0;
questions.outputSpec: No result set is read. The final contents of Trades (all columns) and MarketQuotes must equal the expected post-update state.

checkQueries.sql: SELECT * FROM Trades ORDER BY trade_id
SELECT * FROM MarketQuotes ORDER BY quote_id

hiddenTests.description: No pending trades have a valid quote (all rejected)
Randomised: mixed statuses and NULL quotes

solution.referenceSolution:
UPDATE Trades
SET status = 'REJECTED'
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM MarketQuotes q
        WHERE q.security_id = Trades.security_id
          AND q.quote_date  = Trades.trade_date
          AND q.bid IS NOT NULL AND q.ask IS NOT NULL
          AND ABS(Trades.price - (q.bid + q.ask) / 2.0) <= 0.05 * ((q.bid + q.ask) / 2.0)
  );
solution.explanation: A correlated NOT EXISTS subquery looks for a supporting quote; if none exists the pending trade is rejected. EXISTS is NULL-safe, whereas `price NOT BETWEEN ...` computed over a LEFT JOIN or `NOT IN` over NULLs would misclassify missing quotes.

questions.title: Clean a Raw Tick Feed
questions.statement:
Raw ticks arrive with inconsistent symbols, bad timestamps, duplicated messages and invalid prices. Implement `clean_ticks(ticks)` which returns a clean tick table.

Apply these steps **in this order**:

1. Normalise `symbol` with `str.strip()` and `str.upper()`.
2. Parse `ts` with format `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`; unparseable values become `NaT`; **drop** those rows.
3. Remove duplicate `(symbol, ts)` pairs, **keeping the last** row in the original input order.
4. Drop rows where `price` is missing or `<= 0`, or where `size <= 0`.
5. Sort by `symbol` then `ts` ascending and reset the index.

Return exactly the columns `symbol, ts, price, size` (`ts` as datetime64). Do not modify the input DataFrame.

def clean_ticks(ticks: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Return the cleaned tick table (see problem statement)."""
    df = ticks.copy()
    # TODO
    return df
questions.outputSpec: DataFrame with columns [symbol (str), ts (datetime64), price (float64), size (int64)], sorted by symbol, ts; default RangeIndex (index is ignored by the grader).

columns.name: symbol
columns.description: Raw symbol, may contain spaces/lower case

columns.name: price
columns.description: Trade price; may be NaN, zero or negative

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: mixed case/whitespace, duplicates, bad timestamps and prices
Duplicate key whose last row has NaN price removes the key

hiddenTests.description: Everything invalid -> empty result with correct columns

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def clean_ticks(ticks):
    df = ticks.copy()
    df["symbol"] = df["symbol"].str.strip().str.upper()
    df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["ts"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["symbol", "ts"], keep="last")
    df = df[df["price"].notna() & (df["price"] > 0) & (df["size"] > 0)]
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "ts"], kind="mergesort")
    return df[["symbol", "ts", "price", "size"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Normalise first so ' AAPL' and 'aapl' collide; parse with errors='coerce' and drop NaT; drop_duplicates(keep='last') on the normalised key; then filter invalid prices/sizes. Because duplicates are removed before price filtering, a last duplicate with a NaN price eliminates the key entirely (a different order would resurrect the earlier row).

1. Convert `date` to datetime and sort by `symbol`, `date` (stable sort).
2. Treat any `close <= 0` as missing.
3. **Within each symbol**, forward-fill missing closes. Leading missing values stay missing – never fill across symbols and never back-fill.
4. `daily_return = close / previous_close_of_same_symbol - 1`, using the filled closes. It is `NaN` for the first row of each symbol and whenever the current or previous filled close is missing.

import pandas as pd

def fill_and_returns(prices):
    df = prices.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "date"], kind="mergesort").reset_index(drop=True)
    df["close"] = df["close"].where(df["close"] > 0)          # non-positive prices are invalid -> missing
    df["close"] = df.groupby("symbol")["close"].ffill()
    prev = df.groupby("symbol")["close"].shift(1)
    df["daily_return"] = df["close"] / prev - 1
    return df[["symbol", "date", "close", "daily_return"]]
solution.explanation: groupby('symbol')['close'].ffill() fills only within symbols; computing the return as close / groupby.shift(1) - 1 gives NaN for first rows and for rows next to a leading gap. Masking close <= 0 before filling makes a zero price behave like a missing one.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def wide_returns(returns):
    df = returns.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    wide = df.pivot_table(index="date", columns="symbol", values="ret", aggfunc="mean", dropna=False)
    wide = wide.reindex(sorted(wide.columns), axis=1)
    out = wide.copy()
    out["market_avg"] = wide.mean(axis=1, skipna=True)
    out["n_reporting"] = wide.notna().sum(axis=1).astype("int64")
    out = out.sort_index().reset_index()
    out.columns.name = None
    return out
solution.explanation: pivot_table with aggfunc='mean' collapses duplicates; dropna=False keeps all-NaN cells. Mean with skipna handles missing symbols; notna().sum(axis=1) counts reporting symbols.
